headline: Echoes are sound waves reflected back—your voice returning to you from a distance
universal_truth: What we put out into the world often comes back to us
fun_facts: You need at least 56 feet of distance to hear a distinct echo—closer than that, sounds blend together
Bats use echolocation to 'see' in darkness, sending out clicks and mapping the world from echoes
The longest echo ever recorded lasted 112 seconds in a Scottish fuel depot
discussion_questions: What 'echoes' do you hear in your life—things you sent out coming back?
How do animals that use echolocation 'see' the world?
What would you say if you knew it would echo forever?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: Shout into a canyon and wait. Your voice returns—sometimes twice, sometimes fading in waves. That's an echo: sound waves that hit a surface and bounced back. You're hearing your own voice after it traveled there and back. It's almost like time travel.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: Sometimes you hear clear echoes; other times sounds just disappear. Why don't all surfaces produce echoes? What makes a canyon echo but a bedroom absorb sound?

options.text: Hard, flat surfaces at sufficient distance that reflect rather than absorb sound
options.response: Yes. Hard surfaces reflect sound; soft surfaces absorb it. Distance separates the echo from the original.

options.text: Quiet environments with little background noise
options.response: Quiet helps you hear it, but the echo itself depends on surfaces...

q1.title: The 56-Foot Rule
q1.script: Sound travels about 1,100 feet per second. Your brain can only distinguish two sounds as separate if they're about 0.1 seconds apart. Do the math: you need at least 56 feet of distance for sound to travel there and back in time to hear a distinct echo.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "The 56-Foot Rule"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Echolocation
q2.script: Bats and dolphins use echolocation—they emit sounds and map their environment from the returning echoes. Bats can detect objects as thin as a human hair using this method. They don't see with eyes in darkness—they see with sound.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: The 112-Second Echo
q3.script: In 2014, a team recorded a 112-second echo in an abandoned Scottish fuel depot—the longest ever. The huge concrete chambers allowed sound to bounce back and forth for nearly two minutes. An echo so long it became a phenomenon.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Life echoes. What you put out—kindness or cruelty, truth or deception—often returns to you. The canyon doesn't judge what you shout; it just sends it back. Be thoughtful about what you send into the world.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 46. Tomorrow, we'll explore how waves carry energy. Until then, find a place with an echo—and listen to your voice return.
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Life Echoes - What Returns to You
growTrack.learning_objective: Notice patterns of what you send out and what comes back
growTrack.activity: Think of something good that has 'echoed' back to you—a kindness that was returned, an effort that paid off. Then think of something negative that echoed. What patterns do you notice? What would you like to send out more of?
